meta.title: IPSC Rules Quiz
meta.source: IPSC Shotgun Competition Rules, January 2026 Edition (Final 29 Dec 2025), International Practical Shooting Confederation

coverage.note: Approximate coverage: the number of distinct numbered rule paragraphs, appendix items and glossary terms referenced by at least one question, against all such numbered items in the source document.

chapterNames.Appendix B2: IPSC Target / Mini Target / Universal Target

questions.q: What three equivalent elements of IPSC shooting are expressed by the Latin words "Diligentia, Vis, Celeritas" (DVC)?
questions.refText: Balance – Accuracy, Power and Speed are equivalent elements of IPSC shooting, and are expressed in the Latin words "Diligentia, Vis, Celeritas" ("DVC").

questions.q: According to the Diversity principle, what must never happen with a single course of fire?
o: It must never be repeated in a way that allows it to be considered a definitive measure of IPSC shooting skills
It must never require more than 8 rounds
It must never include moving targets
It must never be shot by more than one Division
questions.refText: Diversity – IPSC shooting challenges are diverse. While it is not necessary to construct new courses for each match, no single course of fire must be repeated to allow its use to be considered a definitive measure of IPSC shooting skills.

questions.q: Under the Freestyle principle, what must courses of fire NOT do after the Start Signal (except as specifically permitted)?
o: Require mandatory reloads or dictate a shooting position, location or stance
Allow competitors to move at all
Require competitors to use ear protection
Include more than one target array
questions.refText: Freestyle – ...After the Start Signal, courses of fire must not require mandatory reloads nor dictate a shooting position, location or stance, except as specified below.

questions.q: Which match levels are NOT required to comply strictly with the freestyle requirements or round count limitations?
o: Level I and Level II matches
Level IV and Level V matches
All match levels must comply strictly
questions.refText: Level I and Level II matches are not required to comply strictly with the freestyle requirements or round count limitations (see Section 1.2).

questions.q: In a Short Course or Classifier with a mandatory reload, when must the reload be completed?
o: After the competitor shoots at his first target, and before he shoots at his final target
Before the competitor shoots at his first target
At any time during the course of fire
questions.refText: Short Courses and Classifiers may include mandatory reloads and may dictate a shooting position, location and/or stance. When a mandatory reload is required, it must be completed after the competitor shoots at his first target, and before he shoots at his final target. Violations are subject to one procedural penalty.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of rounds a Short Course may require to complete?
questions.refText: Short Courses – Must not require more than 8 rounds to complete and are restricted to a maximum of 12 scoring hits.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of scoring hits permitted for a Short Course?
questions.refText: Short Courses – Must not require more than 8 rounds to complete and are restricted to a maximum of 12 scoring hits.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of rounds a Medium Course may require to complete?
questions.refText: Medium Courses – Must not require more than 16 rounds to complete and are restricted to a maximum of 24 scoring hits. Course design and construction must not require more than 8 rounds to be shot from any single location or view.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of rounds a Long Course may require to complete?
questions.refText: Long Courses – Must not require more than 28 rounds to complete and are restricted to a maximum of 32 scoring hits. Course design and construction must not require more than 8 rounds to be shot from any single location or view. A COF requiring 24 or more rounds must not stipulate an unloaded gun as a start condition.

questions.q: A course of fire requiring 24 or more rounds must not stipulate what as a start condition?
questions.refText: A COF requiring 24 or more rounds must not stipulate an unloaded gun as a start condition.

questions.q: What is the approved ratio of Short Courses to Medium Courses to Long Courses for an IPSC sanctioned match?
questions.refText: The approved balance for an IPSC sanctioned match is a ratio of 3 Short Courses to 2 Medium Courses to 1 Long Course (see Approved Stage Ratios in Appendix A4).

questions.q: For no more than what percentage of the courses of fire in a match should an empty chamber and/or empty magazine well/cylinder ready condition be required?
questions.refText: Empty chamber and/or empty magazine well/cylinder firearm ready conditions (see Chapter 8), should not be required for more than 25% of the courses of fire in a match.

questions.q: What is a Classifier?
o: A course of fire authorized by a Regional Director and/or IPSC, available to competitors seeking a regional and/or international classification
A course reserved exclusively for Level IV or higher matches
A course of fire used only in a Shoot-Off
questions.refText: Classifiers – Courses of fire authorized by a Regional Director and/or IPSC, which are available to competitors seeking a regional and/or international classification.

questions.q: In a Shoot-Off, what is the maximum number of rounds each target array must not exceed?
questions.refText: Shoot-Off – ...Each target array must not exceed 8 rounds and each competitor may be required to perform a mandatory reload after shooting at his first target, and before he shoots at his final target. Violations are subject to automatic forfeiture of the bout.

questions.q: In a Shoot-Off, what happens if a competitor violates the mandatory reload requirement?
questions.refText: Shoot-Off – ...each competitor may be required to perform a mandatory reload after shooting at his first target, and before he shoots at his final target. Violations are subject to automatic forfeiture of the bout.

questions.q: Who may withdraw IPSC sanctioning from a match, and in what order of precedence?
o: The IPSC President, his delegate, or an officer of the Confederation, in that order
The Match Director, then the Range Master
questions.refText: The IPSC President, his delegate, or an officer of the Confederation (in that order), may withdraw IPSC sanctioning from a match if...

questions.q: Where are IPSC match level requirements and recommendations specified?
questions.refText: IPSC match level requirements and recommendations are specified in Appendix A1.

questions.q: Unless otherwise specified, what is the default maximum muzzle angle, measured from the front of the competitor facing directly center downrange?
questions.refText: Unless otherwise specified, the default maximum muzzle angle is 90 degrees in all directions, measured from the front of the competitor facing directly center downrange. Violations are subject to Rule 10.5.2.

questions.q: What is the minimum distance for shooting metal targets or metal hard cover with birdshot or buckshot?
questions.refText: Minimum Distances for Shooting Birdshot and Buckshot – The minimum distance is 5 meters. Fault Lines must be placed at least 6 meters from the targets or metal hard cover.

questions.q: If Fault Lines are used to limit approach to metal targets when shooting birdshot or buckshot, at what minimum distance must they be placed from the targets?
questions.refText: Minimum Distances for Shooting Birdshot and Buckshot – The minimum distance is 5 meters. Fault Lines must be placed at least 6 meters from the targets or metal hard cover.

questions.q: What is the minimum distance for shooting metal targets or metal hard cover with slugs?
questions.refText: Minimum Distances for Shooting Slugs – The minimum distance is 40 meters. Fault Lines must be placed at least 41 meters from the targets or metal hard cover.

questions.q: In a course of fire with a common firing line where multiple competitors fire simultaneously (e.g. a Shoot-Off), what minimum free space must be provided between each competitor?
questions.refText: Common Firing Lines – Courses of fire where multiple competitors are required to fire simultaneously from a common firing line (e.g. Shoot-Off), must provide a minimum of 3 meters of free space between each competitor.

questions.q: Static targets (those which are not activated) must not be presented at an angle greater than how many degrees from the vertical?
questions.refText: Static targets (i.e. those which are not activated) must not be presented at an angle greater than 90 degrees from the vertical.

questions.q: Areas designated as berms are considered:
o: "Off limits" to all persons at all times, except when access is specifically permitted by a Range Officer
Accessible to all competitors between stages
questions.refText: Berms – All berms are "off limits" to all persons at all times, except when access to them is specifically permitted by a Range Officer (see Section 10.6).

questions.q: What backing distance is recommended for paper targets when shooting buckshot, to prevent detachable wads penetrating them?
questions.refText: Detachable Wads – ...In view of this paper targets should either be "backed" ...or placed at a greater distance. 10 meters is recommended in the case of buckshot, to prevent such wads penetrating paper targets.

questions.q: A competitor must never be required to engage paper targets using what type of ammunition?
questions.refText: Birdshot Ammunition with Paper Targets – A competitor must never be required to engage paper targets using birdshot ammunition.

questions.q: How many types of permitted ammunition must a course of fire nominate?
o: A single permitted type (birdshot, buckshot or slugs)
Any combination the Match Director prefers
questions.refText: Permitted Ammunition – Courses of fire must nominate a single permitted type of ammunition, i.e. birdshot, buckshot or slugs.

questions.q: Fault Lines must rise at least how far above ground level?
questions.refText: Fault Lines must be fixed firmly in place, they must rise at least 2 centimeters above ground level, they should be constructed of wood or other rigid materials, and they should be of a consistent color (preferably red).

questions.q: Unless used continuously to define the boundary of a shooting area, what is the minimum length of a Fault Line?
questions.refText: Unless used in a continuous manner to define the boundary of a general shooting area, Fault Lines must be a minimum of 1.5 meters in length, but they are deemed to extend to infinity.

questions.q: If a competitor takes a shortcut outside a passageway or shooting area clearly delineated by Fault Lines, what penalty applies?
o: One procedural penalty total, regardless of shots fired
One procedural penalty for each shot fired after beginning the shortcut
No penalty unless a target is missed
questions.refText: If a COF has a passageway visibly delineated by Fault Lines and/or a clearly demarcated shooting area, any competitor who takes a shortcut by stepping on the ground outside the passageway and/or shooting area will incur one procedural penalty for each shot fired after beginning the shortcut.

questions.q: Unless supplemented by a shooting platform or similar, barriers of at least what height are deemed to extend skywards to infinity?
questions.refText: They must be high enough and strong enough to serve the intended purpose. Unless supplemented by a shooting platform or similar, barriers of at least 1.8 meters high are deemed to extend skywards to infinity (also see Rule 10.2.11).

questions.q: What are Cooper Tunnels?
o: Tunnels comprised of braced uprights supporting loose overhead materials, which may fall off when inadvertently dislodged
Underground passages used only in Level IV or higher matches
A type of metal hard cover
A protective structure required around all chronograph stations
questions.refText: Cooper Tunnels – Are tunnels comprised of braced uprights supporting loose overhead materials (e.g. wooden slats), which may fall off when inadvertently dislodged by competitors (see Rule 10.2.5).

questions.q: Windows and ports in a course of fire must be placed at a height reachable by most competitors, with what being made available for others without penalty, if requested?
questions.refText: Windows and Ports – Must be placed at a height reachable by most competitors, with a sturdy platform being available for use by others, if requested, without penalty.

questions.q: Any physical changes or additions the Range Master approves to a published course of fire should be completed:
o: Only after all competitors have shot the stage
Only at the start of each match day
Within 24 hours of the match's conclusion
questions.refText: Match Officials may, for any reason, modify the physical construction or stage procedure for a course of fire, provided that such changes are approved in advance by the Range Master. Any such physical changes or additions to a published course of fire should be completed before the stage begins.

questions.q: A competitor who refuses to reshoot a course of fire when so ordered by a Range Officer will receive:
o: A zero score for that stage, irrespective of any previous attempt
questions.refText: A competitor who refuses to reshoot a course of fire, under this or any other Section, when so ordered by a Range Officer, will receive a zero score for that stage, irrespective of any previous attempt.

questions.q: During inclement weather, an order by the Range Master that paper targets be fitted with transparent protective covers and/or overhead shelters is:
o: Not subject to appeal by competitors
Only valid for the remainder of that day
Subject to a vote of all competitors
questions.refText: During inclement weather, the Range Master may order that paper targets be fitted with transparent protective covers and/or overhead shelters, and this order is not subject to appeal by competitors (see Rule 6.6.1).

questions.q: Safety Areas at tournaments and long gun matches must include what, adjacent to but not inside the Safety Area?
o: Sufficient gun racks for secure muzzle-up storage of rifles and shotguns
questions.refText: Safety Areas at tournaments and long gun matches must include sufficient gun racks adjacent to, but not in, the Safety Area for secure muzzle-up storage of rifles and shotguns.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the activities competitors are permitted to conduct unsupervised in a Safety Area?
o: Casing, uncasing, and holstering unloaded firearms
Handling loose live ammunition to inspect it
Practicing mounting, drawing and dry firing unloaded firearms
Cleaning and maintenance of firearms and component parts
questions.refText: Competitors are permitted to use Safety Areas unsupervised for the activities stated below... Dummy ammunition and live rounds, whether loose, packaged or contained in magazines or speed loaders, must not be handled in a Safety Area under any circumstances (see Rule 10.5.13).

questions.q: At Level III or higher tournaments and long gun matches, a test firing bay should include approved targets to assist competitors in:
questions.refText: At Level III or higher tournaments and long gun matches, approved IPSC paper and metal targets ...should be available for use by competitors to aid in the sighting-in of their firearms, in accordance with the guidelines shown in Appendix C3.

questions.q: Before being displayed by a vendor, assembled firearms must be:
o: Fitted with a chamber safety flag only
questions.refText: Vendors...are solely responsible for the safe handling and security of their products and other items in their care, and ensuring they are displayed in a condition that will not endanger any person. Assembled firearms must be deactivated prior to being displayed.

questions.q: Hygiene areas with hand cleansing supplies should be provided adjacent to lavatories and near the entrance to:
questions.refText: A sufficient number of hygiene areas, with hand cleansing supplies and facilities, should be provided adjacent to lavatories and near the entrance to food service areas.

questions.q: For Published Courses of Fire, registered competitors and/or their Regional Directors must be provided with course of fire information:
o: Within the same notice period, in advance of the match
Only once the match has begun
questions.refText: Published Courses of Fire – Registered competitors and/or their Regional Directors must be provided with the same course of fire information, within the same notice period, in advance of the match.

questions.q: For a Non-Published Course of Fire, where are the course of fire instructions provided?
o: On the official match website only
Only verbally by the Match Director
They are never provided in advance or at the stage
questions.refText: Non-Published Courses of Fire – Same as Rule 3.1.1 except that the details for the course of fire are not published beforehand. The course of fire instructions are provided in the written stage briefing.

questions.q: Which of the following is required minimum information in a written stage briefing for a Shotgun match?
o: The name of the Chief Range Officer
questions.refText: A written stage briefing...must provide the following minimum information: ...Ammunition type (Shotgun matches only)...

questions.q: How must the Range Officer in charge of a course of fire deliver the written stage briefing to each squad?
o: Summarize it in his own words
Post it silently on a noticeboard only
Only demonstrate the start position without reading it
questions.refText: The Range Officer in charge of a course of fire must read out the written stage briefing verbatim to each squad. The Range Officer must visually demonstrate the acceptable Start Position (either by use of a picture or physically) at all match levels.

questions.q: During the walkthrough (course inspection), the duration of time for the inspection must be:
o: Stipulated by the Range Officer and the same for all competitors
questions.refText: ...competitors should be permitted to conduct an orderly inspection ("walkthrough") of the course of fire. The duration of time for the inspection must be stipulated by the Range Officer, and it should be the same for all competitors.

questions.q: Host organizations may enforce local rules at IPSC matches only to comply with:
o: Legislation or legal precedent in the applicable jurisdiction
questions.refText: IPSC matches are governed by the rules applicable to the discipline. Host organizations may not enforce local rules except to comply with legislation or legal precedent in the applicable jurisdiction.

questions.q: Which types of targets, besides those fully complying with Appendices B and C, may be used in IPSC Shotgun matches?
o: Targets improvised on site by the Range Officer
questions.refText: Only targets approved by the IPSC Assembly and which fully comply with the specifications in Appendices B and C, and frangible targets (see Rule 4.5.1), are to be used for IPSC Shotgun matches.

questions.q: Which combination of target types is prohibited from being included together in the same target array?
o: IPSC Targets and IPSC Mini Targets
IPSC Mini Targets and IPSC Mini Poppers
IPSC Targets and IPSC Mini Poppers
questions.refText: The following types and sizes of targets must not be included together in the same target array: IPSC Targets and IPSC Mini Targets; or IPSC Poppers and IPSC Mini Poppers.

questions.q: What color must the scoring area of the IPSC Target and Mini Target be, unless a lack of contrast requires otherwise?
questions.refText: The scoring area of the IPSC Target and Mini Target must be tan colored, except where the Range Master deems that a lack of contrast with the surrounding area or background necessitates that a different color be used.

questions.q: No-shoot targets must be clearly marked with what, or be of a single unique color different from scoring targets?
questions.refText: No-shoots must be clearly marked with a conspicuous "X" or be of a single, unique color different from scoring targets throughout a match or tournament.

questions.q: Hard cover used to hide all or part of a target must not be:
o: In the shape of a whole IPSC target
A different color from the target
questions.refText: Cover provided to hide all or a portion of a target will be considered hard cover... Hard cover must not be in the shape of a whole IPSC target.

questions.q: Attaching a Mini Target to a full size target, or declaring one intact target to represent two or more targets, is:
o: Permitted only in Level I and II matches
questions.refText: Declaring a single, intact target to represent two or more targets by use of tape, paint or any other means and/or attaching a Mini Target to a full size target is prohibited.

questions.q: How many paper targets are approved for use in IPSC Shotgun matches?
questions.refText: There are five paper targets approved for use in IPSC Shotgun matches (see Appendix B).

questions.q: What is the width of the non-scoring border on a standard (non-Mini) IPSC paper target?
questions.refText: Paper targets must have scoring lines and 0.5 cm (Mini Targets 0.3 cm) non-scoring borders clearly marked on the front of the target.

questions.q: Scoring lines and non-scoring borders on paper targets should not be visible beyond what distance?
questions.refText: Paper targets must have scoring lines and 0.5 cm...non-scoring borders clearly marked on the front of the target. However, scoring lines and non-scoring borders should not be visible beyond a distance of 10 meters.

questions.q: Hard cover (and overlapping no-shoots) must not completely hide what zone on a partially hidden paper target?
o: Any zone, as long as some part remains visible
questions.refText: Hard cover (and overlapping no-shoots) must not completely hide the A zone on a partially hidden paper target.

questions.q: Metal targets and no-shoots which can accidentally turn edge-on or sideways when hit are:
o: Expressly prohibited, and using them may result in withdrawal of IPSC sanction
Permitted in Level I matches only
Permitted if approved by the Range Master
questions.refText: Metal targets and no-shoots which can accidentally turn edge-on or sideways when hit are expressly prohibited. Using them may result in withdrawal of IPSC sanction.

questions.q: Metal targets and no-shoots must do what to score?
o: Be shot and fall, overturn or self-indicate
Simply be struck by any part of the pattern
questions.refText: Metal targets and no-shoots must be shot and fall, overturn or self-indicate to score.

questions.q: If a metal plate fails to fall or overturn when initially hit, but falls or overturns when hit with a subsequent shot, is this subject to a reshoot?
o: No, it is not subject to a reshoot
Only at Level III or higher matches
Only if the Range Master approves
questions.refText: Metal plates which fail to fall or overturn when initially hit, but which fall or overturn when hit with a subsequent shot, are not subject to a reshoot.

questions.q: Frangible targets, such as clay pigeons or tiles, may be used in IPSC Shotgun matches as:
o: Scoring targets, but not as no-shoots
Both scoring targets and no-shoots equally
questions.refText: Frangible targets, such as clay pigeons or tiles, may be used as scoring targets, but not as no-shoots, in IPSC Shotgun matches.

questions.q: Synthetic ("self-sealing") targets must not be used at:
o: Any indoor range regardless of level
questions.refText: Synthetic targets (e.g. "self-sealing" targets etc.), sometimes used by indoor ranges, must not be used at Level III or higher matches. However, subject to the prior written approval of a Regional Director, synthetic targets may be used at Level I and II matches held within his Region.

questions.q: A competitor who interferes with the range surface, natural foliage, constructions, props or other range equipment may incur:
o: One procedural penalty per occurrence, at the discretion of the Range Officer
A mandatory reshoot regardless of penalty
No penalty unless equipment is damaged
questions.refText: The competitor must not interfere with the range surface, natural foliage, constructions, props or other range equipment...at any time. Violations may incur one procedural penalty per occurrence at the discretion of the Range Officer.

questions.q: Range equipment failure includes, but is not limited to, which of the following?
o: Displacement of paper targets and premature activation of metal or moving targets
A competitor using the wrong ammunition type
questions.refText: Range equipment failure includes, but is not limited to, the displacement of paper targets, the premature activation of metal or moving targets, the malfunction of mechanically or electrically operated equipment, and the failure of props such as openings, ports, and barriers.

questions.q: Are unrestored paper targets (not properly patched between competitors) considered range equipment failure?
o: No, unrestored paper targets are not range equipment failure
Only at Level IV or higher matches
Only if the Range Master declares them so
questions.refText: Unrestored paper targets are not range equipment failure (see Rule 9.1.4).

questions.q: Chronic malfunction of equipment in a course of fire may result in:
o: The removal of that stage from the match results
A warning to the Quartermaster only
Automatic disqualification of the affected competitor
questions.refText: Chronic malfunction of equipment in a course of fire may result in the removal of that stage from the match results (see Rule 2.3.4).

questions.q: What is the minimum caliber for shotguns used in IPSC matches?
questions.refText: The minimum caliber for shotguns used in IPSC matches is 20 gauge (20 bore).

questions.q: Are laser sights permitted in IPSC Shotgun matches?
o: Yes, but only in Open Division
Yes, but only for competitors with a disability dispensation
questions.refText: "Laser sights" are aiming devices fitted to a firearm that project a beam onto the target, providing a visual reference point. They are not permitted in IPSC matches.

questions.q: Triggers and/or trigger shoes that extend beyond the width of the trigger guard are:
o: Expressly prohibited, except properly fitted "winter triggers/guards" for climate reasons
Permitted with Range Master approval only
questions.refText: Triggers and/or trigger shoes that extend beyond the width of the trigger guard are expressly prohibited. However, shotguns fitted with "winter triggers/guards" may be used in this mode, provided that this fitting was designed, manufactured and provided as part of the shotgun and only when the particular climate or weather conditions dictate their use.

questions.q: A competitor must use the same firearm, barrel and type of sights for:
o: All courses of fire in a match
questions.refText: Competitors must use the same firearm, barrel and type of sights for all courses of fire in a match. This includes magazine tubes which must not be changed unless they are changed as part of routine reloading during a course of fire.

questions.q: A competitor must never use or wear on his person how many firearms during a course of fire?
questions.refText: A competitor must never use or wear on his person more than one firearm during a course of fire (see Rule 10.5.8).

questions.q: The shotgun must be fitted with what to enable it to be fired from the shoulder?
questions.refText: The shotgun must be fitted with a stock enabling it to be fired from the shoulder (see Rule 10.5.16).

questions.q: Firearms offering "burst" and/or fully automatic operation are:
o: Permitted for law enforcement competitors only
Permitted with a Regional Director waiver
questions.refText: Firearms offering "burst" and/or fully automatic operation (i.e. whereby more than one round can be discharged on a single pull or activation of the trigger) are prohibited.

questions.q: Combination guns offering an additional barrel that is not a conventional shotgun barrel (e.g. a shotgun and rifle combination) are:
o: Permitted with a barrel change between stages
questions.refText: Combination guns offering an additional barrel, or barrels, that is not a conventional shotgun barrel (e.g. a shotgun and rifle combination) are prohibited.

questions.q: Outside a Safety Area or Range Officer supervision, long guns must be carried unloaded and held, shouldered, slung or racked, with the muzzle pointed:
o: In any safe direction chosen by the competitor
questions.refText: Carry and Storage – Except when within the boundaries of a Safety Area, or when under the supervision and direct command of a Range Officer, long guns must be unloaded and held, shouldered or slung (or placed in a rack), with the muzzle pointed skywards.

questions.q: A competitor arriving at an IPSC match in possession of a loaded firearm must:
o: Immediately report to a Range Officer, who will supervise unloading
Report only if asked by another competitor
questions.refText: Competitors arriving at an IPSC match in possession of a loaded firearm must immediately report to a Range Officer, who will supervise unloading of the firearm. Competitors failing to comply may be subject to Rule 10.5.14.

questions.q: Which type of ammunition carrier is expressly prohibited for a competitor's equipment belt?
questions.refText: Unless otherwise specified in the written stage briefing the competitor's equipment belt carrying cartridges (in caddies, loops, clips, bags or pouches) and/or detachable magazines and/or speed loaders must be worn at waist level. "Chest-rigs", bandoliers and similar carriers are expressly prohibited.

questions.q: Cartridges held in loops or clips on the competitor's belt are restricted to what maximum total height?
questions.refText: Only one equipment carrying belt is permitted. Cartridges held in loops or clips on the belt are restricted to a maximum of 170 mm total height. Rounds carried in caddies (often known as "strippers") must not exceed 6 rounds in height.

questions.q: When carried in loops, clips or caddies, no part of any cartridge is permitted to extend further than what distance from a competitor's belt?
questions.refText: When carried in loops, clips or caddies no part of any cartridge is permitted to extend further than 75 mm from a competitor's belt... Open Division competitors are exempt from this rule.

questions.q: Which competitors are exempt from the 75 mm maximum cartridge protrusion rule?
questions.refText: When carried in loops, clips or caddies no part of any cartridge is permitted to extend further than 75 mm from a competitor's belt. Cartridges carried on the gun are exempt and loose cartridges carried in a pouch or bag are usually exempt from this rule. The Range Master's decision will be final in this matter. Open Division competitors are exempt from this rule.

questions.q: The use of camouflage or similar military/police garments by competitors who are not law enforcement or military personnel is:
o: Required at Level IV and higher matches
Permitted only in Standard Manual Division
questions.refText: The use of camouflage or other similar types of military or police garments other than by competitors who are law enforcement or military personnel is discouraged. The Match Director will be the final authority in respect of what garments must not be worn by competitors.

questions.q: If a Range Officer notices a competitor has lost or displaced eye or ear protection during a course of fire, the competitor:
o: Must be immediately stopped and will be required to reshoot after the protective devices are restored
Continues shooting but receives a procedural penalty
Is warned only, with no reshoot
questions.refText: If a Range Officer notices that a competitor has lost or displaced their eye or ear protection during a course of fire, or has commenced a course of fire without them, the Range Officer must immediately stop the competitor who will be required to reshoot the course of fire after the protective devices have been restored.

questions.q: Any attempt to gain a reshoot or advantage by removing eye and/or ear protection during a course of fire is considered:
o: Grounds for a warning on the first occurrence only
questions.refText: Any attempt to gain a reshoot or advantage by removing eye and/or ear protection during a course of fire will be considered unsportsmanlike conduct (see Rule 10.6.2).

questions.q: What type of ammunition is prohibited at IPSC matches?
o: Metal piercing, incendiary and/or tracer ammunition
questions.refText: Metal piercing, incendiary and/or tracer ammunition is prohibited at IPSC matches (see Rule 10.5.16).

questions.q: Cartridges using specialized long-range wads are:
o: Prohibited; only conventional wads are permitted
Permitted only in slug courses of fire
questions.refText: Only cartridges using conventional wads are permitted. Cartridges using specialized long-range wads (see Glossary) are prohibited (see Rule 10.5.16).

questions.q: Cartridges exceeding what power factor are prohibited?
questions.refText: Cartridges exceeding a power factor of 750 are prohibited. The cartridge power factor is calculated either by reference to the manufacturer's published data or determined by the use of a chronograph.

questions.q: Cartridges with steel or tungsten based shot or slugs are deemed unsafe for shooting at:
questions.refText: Cartridges with steel or tungsten based shot or slugs are deemed unsafe for shooting at metal targets (see Rule 10.5.16).

questions.q: All rounds loaded in the shotgun prior to the Start Signal must be:
o: Of the same configuration (wad, velocity, propellant, pellet weight, pellet size, length, etc.)
Of any configuration the competitor chooses
Verified by the Range Officer individually
questions.refText: All rounds loaded in the shotgun prior to the Start Signal must be of the same configuration (i.e. wad, velocity, propellant, pellet weight, pellet size, length, etc.). Violations may be subject to Rule 10.6.1.

questions.q: At the beginning of the first day of a match, how many rounds are fired through the calibration firearm to verify the chronograph?
questions.refText: At the beginning of the first day of the match, a Range Officer will fire 3 rounds from the supply of the official match calibration ammunition through the calibration firearm over the chronograph, and the average velocity of the 3 rounds will be recorded.

questions.q: The chronograph will be deemed within tolerance if the daily average velocity is within what percentage of the Day 1 average?
questions.refText: The chronograph will be deemed to be within tolerance if the daily average velocity is within +/- 5% of the average velocity achieved in Rule 5.6.2.1.

questions.q: How many sample rounds are initially drawn from a competitor for the chronograph test?
questions.refText: An initial 8 sample rounds for the chronograph test will be drawn from the competitor at a time and place determined by Match Officials, who may require additional tests of a competitor's ammunition at any time during the match.

questions.q: How is Power Factor calculated according to Rule 5.6.3.5?
o: Weight of projectiles (grains) x velocity (feet per second), divided by 1000
Weight of projectiles (grams) x velocity (meters per second)
Velocity (fps) divided by weight of projectiles (grains)
Weight of projectiles (grains) plus velocity (feet per second)
questions.refText: Power Factor is calculated using the actual weight of the projectile(s) and the average velocity of the 3 rounds fired, according to the following formula: Power Factor = weight of projectiles (grains) x velocity (feet per second) / 1000.

questions.q: For the final power factor calculation, decimal places are:
o: Ignored (e.g. a result of 479.999 is not 480)
Rounded to the nearest whole number
questions.refText: The final result will ignore all decimal places (e.g. for IPSC purposes, a result of 479.999 is not 480).

questions.q: During a firearm malfunction after the Start Signal, what must a competitor NOT use to verify or correct the malfunction?
questions.refText: If a competitor's firearm malfunctions after the Start Signal, the competitor may safely attempt to correct the problem and continue the course of fire...The competitor must not use rods or other tools to verify or correct the malfunction. Violations will result in a zero score for the stage.

questions.q: If a firearm malfunction cannot be corrected by the competitor within how many minutes, the Range Officer will terminate the course of fire?
questions.refText: In the event that a firearm malfunction cannot be corrected by the competitor within 2 minutes, or if the competitor self-stops for any other reason, he must point the firearm safely downrange and advise the Range Officer, who will terminate the course of fire in the normal manner.

questions.q: Under no circumstances is a competitor permitted to leave a course of fire in possession of:
questions.refText: Under no circumstances is a competitor permitted to leave a course of fire in the possession of a loaded firearm (see Rule 10.5.14).

questions.q: Malfunctions of official match ammunition purchased by competitors are deemed to be competitor equipment issues, and therefore:
o: Will not be grounds for a reshoot and/or an appeal to Arbitration
Result in disqualification of the competitor
Must be reported to the IPSC President
questions.refText: Official match ammunition purchased by competitors is deemed to be competitor equipment (see Section 5.7), therefore malfunctions will not be grounds for a reshoot and/or an appeal to Arbitration.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of stages that must make up an IPSC Match, where all stages use the same type of firearm?
questions.refText: Match – Consists of a minimum of 3 stages where all stages use the same type of firearm. The total sum of individual stage results will be accumulated to declare a match winner.

questions.q: What is a Tournament, as defined in the rules?
o: A special match where individual stages are assigned to one particular type of firearm (e.g. some stages Handgun, others Rifle, others Shotgun)
Any match with more than 12 stages
A match reserved exclusively for Level IV or higher competitors
A single stage shot by multiple firearm types simultaneously
questions.refText: Tournament – A special match where individual stages are assigned to one particular type of firearm (e.g. Stages 1-4 Handgun, Stages 5-8 Rifle, Stages 9-12 Shotgun). The total sum of individual stage results will be accumulated to declare a tournament winner.

questions.q: What is a Grand Tournament?
o: Two or more firearm specific matches (e.g. a handgun match and a shotgun match) combined to declare an overall winner
A single match consisting of more than 30 stages
A match reserved for Regional Teams only
questions.refText: Grand Tournament – Consists of two or more firearm specific matches (e.g. a handgun match and a shotgun match, or a handgun match, a rifle match and a shotgun match). The individual match results achieved by a competitor in each component match will be used to declare an overall tournament winner.

questions.q: A Region affiliated to IPSC that wishes to sanction a shooting match within the geographical boundaries of another Region must obtain:
o: The advance and written approval of the Regional Director of the Region where the match is to be held
Approval only from the IPSC President
No approval; any Region may sanction a match anywhere
Approval from a simple majority vote of the IPSC Assembly
questions.refText: A Region affiliated to IPSC cannot actively or passively sanction a shooting match of any type or format within the geographical boundaries of another Region without the advance and written approval of the Regional Director of the Region where the match is to be held.

questions.q: When multiple Divisions are available in a match, how must scoring be handled?
o: Each Division must be scored separately and independently, with a winner recognized in each
All Divisions are combined into a single overall ranking
Only the largest Division is officially scored
Divisions are scored together unless the Match Director objects
questions.refText: IPSC Divisions recognize different firearms and equipment (see Appendix D). Each match must recognize at least one Division. When multiple Divisions are available in a match, each Division must be scored separately and independently, and match results must recognize a winner in each Division.

questions.q: A competitor entering a match in more than one Division may compete for score in:
o: Only one Division, and it must be the first attempt in all cases
Any two Divisions of his choosing
All Divisions he is equipped for
questions.refText: Subject to the prior approval of the Match Director, a competitor may enter a match in more than one Division. However, the competitor may compete for score in only one Division, and that must be the first attempt in all cases.

questions.q: A competitor who fails to satisfy the maximum cartridge-distance-from-body requirement (Rule 5.2.5) after the Start Signal will, on the first offense, incur:
o: A zero score for the stage
questions.refText: A competitor who fails to satisfy the maximum distance of cartridges from his body (see Rule 5.2.5) requirement after the Start Signal will incur a warning for the first offense. Subsequent occurrences in the same match will result in the competitor being placed in Open Division, if available, otherwise the competitor's scores will not be entered into match results.

questions.q: How many Categories may a competitor declare for a single match or tournament?
o: As many as they qualify for
questions.refText: IPSC matches may include different Categories within each Division to recognize different groups of competitors. A competitor may declare only one Category for a match or tournament.

questions.q: With the exception of Family Teams, what is the maximum number of members in a team, of which only the top scores count?
o: 3 members, with the 2 highest scores used
4 members, with the 3 highest scores used
5 members, with the 4 highest scores used
questions.refText: With the exception of Family Teams, teams consist of a maximum of 4 members. However, only the final scores of the 3 highest scoring team members will be used to calculate team results.

questions.q: How many members make up a Family Team?
questions.refText: Family Teams consist of 2 members (see Appendix A2).

questions.q: If a member of a team retires from the match before completing all stages, what happens to the team's score?
o: Scores already attained continue to stand towards the team score, but the team may not replace that member
The team may freely replace the retired member
The team's total score is halved
questions.refText: If a member of a team retires from the match for any reason before completing all of the stages, scores attained by that competitor will continue to stand towards the team score. However, the affected team is not entitled to replace the retired team member.

questions.q: If a member of a team is disqualified from a match, what happens to that member's scores for team purposes, and can the team replace them?
o: The disqualified member's scores revert to zero for all stages, and the team may not replace them
Only the stage where the disqualification occurred is zeroed, and a replacement is allowed
Scores stand as shot and the team is unaffected
questions.refText: If a member of a team is disqualified from a match, the disqualified member's scores will revert to zero for all stages. Teams will not be entitled to replace a disqualified team member.

questions.q: For residency purposes, a competitor must be ordinarily domiciled in a Region for a minimum of how many days of the twelve months preceding the match?
questions.refText: Residency is defined as the Region where the individual is ordinarily domiciled for a minimum of 183 days of the twelve months immediately preceding the month in which the match begins.

questions.q: A competitor who is not present at the scheduled time and date for a stage may not attempt that stage without prior approval of the Match Director, failing which:
o: The competitor's score for that stage will be zero
The competitor is disqualified from the match
The competitor receives a procedural penalty only
The stage is deleted from all results
questions.refText: Competitors must compete for score according to the published match and squadding schedule. A competitor who is not present at the scheduled time and date for any stage may not attempt that stage without the prior approval of the Match Director, failing which the competitor's score for that stage will be zero.

questions.q: Competitors seeking an international classification under the International Classification System (ICS) must use:
o: Approved courses of fire available from the IPSC website
Any course of fire they design themselves
Only courses used at Level V matches
Courses approved solely by their Regional Director
questions.refText: Competitors seeking an international classification must use the approved courses of fire available from the IPSC website.

questions.q: Which Match Official issues range commands and closely monitors safe competitor action, declaring time, scores and penalties?
questions.refText: Range Officer ("RO") – Issues range commands, oversees competitor compliance with the written stage briefing and closely monitors safe competitor action. He also declares the time, scores and penalties achieved by each competitor and verifies that these are correctly recorded on the competitor's score sheet.

questions.q: Which Match Official supervises the stats room team that collects, tabulates and retains score sheets to produce results?
questions.refText: Stats Officer ("SO") – Supervises the stats room team, which collects, sorts, verifies, tabulates and retains all score sheets and ultimately produces provisional and final results.

questions.q: Which Match Official distributes, repairs and maintains range equipment such as targets, patches, timers and staplers?
questions.refText: Quartermaster ("QM") – Distributes, repairs and maintains all range equipment (e.g. targets, patches, paint, props etc.), other range needs (e.g. timers, batteries, staplers, staples, clipboards etc.) and replenishes Range Officer refreshments.

questions.q: Which Match Official has overall authority over all persons and activities within the entire range, including range safety and the application of the rules?
questions.refText: Range Master ("RM") – Has overall authority over all persons and activities within the entire range, including range safety, the operation of all courses of fire and the application of these rules. All disqualifications and appeals to arbitration must be brought to his attention.

questions.q: For IPSC sanctioned Level IV or higher matches, the appointment of the Range Master is subject to:
o: The prior written approval of the IPSC Executive Council
Approval from the host Region's government only
questions.refText: The Range Master is usually appointed by and works with the Match Director. However, in respect of IPSC sanctioned Level IV or higher matches, the appointment of the Range Master is subject to the prior written approval of the IPSC Executive Council.

questions.q: Which Match Official handles overall match administration including squadding, scheduling, range construction and coordination of support staff?
questions.refText: Match Director ("MD") – Handles overall match administration including squadding, scheduling, range construction, the coordination of all support staff and the provision of services.

questions.q: For Level I and II matches, may a single person be appointed both Match Director and Range Master?
o: Only for Level I matches, not Level II
Only with IPSC Executive Council approval
questions.refText: Match organizers must, prior to commencement of a match, appoint a Match Director and a Range Master to carry out the duties detailed in these rules...For Level I and II matches a single person may be appointed to be both the Match Director and the Range Master.

questions.q: A person acting as a Match Official is prohibited from having a holstered firearm while:
o: Directly accompanying and timing a competitor during his attempt at a COF
questions.refText: A person acting as a Match Official is prohibited from having a holstered firearm while directly accompanying and timing a competitor during his attempt at a COF. Violations are subject to Rule 7.2.2.

questions.q: Which shotgun ready condition describes: magazine filled and fitted, chamber(s) loaded, hammer/sear cocked and safety catch applied?
o: There is no such standard condition
questions.refText: Loaded (Option 1): magazine filled and fitted (if applicable), chamber(s) loaded, hammer and/or sear cocked and safety catch applied (if the shotgun is designed to have one).

questions.q: In the Unloaded (Option 3) ready condition, what must be true of the shotgun's magazine and chamber?
o: Fixed magazine empty, detachable magazines removed, and chamber(s) empty
Both magazine and chamber loaded but action open
questions.refText: Unloaded (Option 3): fixed magazine must be empty, detachable magazines removed and chamber(s) must be empty. The action/bolt may be open or closed.

questions.q: Standing erect with the shotgun held in both hands, stock touching the competitor at hip level, barrel parallel to the ground, and fingers outside the trigger guard describes:
o: The standard two-handed competitor ready condition (Rule 8.2.2.1)
An alternative starting position requiring Range Master approval
The position used only during malfunction clearance
questions.refText: Standing erect with the shotgun in the ready condition held in both hands, stock touching the competitor at hip level, barrel parallel to the ground, trigger guard downwards, muzzle pointing downrange and with the fingers outside the trigger guard (see Appendix E1).

questions.q: Unless otherwise stated in the written stage briefing, holding the gun upside down at the start position is:
questions.refText: Unless otherwise stated in the written stage briefing holding the gun upside down is prohibited.

questions.q: A course of fire must never permit a competitor to start a stage with the shotgun in what condition?
o: Mounted into the shoulder and pointing towards targets
questions.refText: A course of fire must never permit a competitor to start a stage with the shotgun mounted into the shoulder and pointing towards targets.

questions.q: After the "Standby" command, how many seconds must the Start Signal follow within?
questions.refText: "Standby" – This command should be followed by the Start Signal within 1 to 4 seconds (also see Rule 10.2.6).

questions.q: A competitor who reacts to the Start Signal but fails to have an official time recorded on the timing device will receive:
o: A zero time and zero score for that stage
A warning and a chance to restart
questions.refText: A competitor who reacts to a Start Signal but, for any reason, does not continue their attempt at the course of fire and fails to have an official time recorded on the timing device operated by the Range Officer, will be given a zero time and zero score for that stage.

questions.q: When performing the final safety check after "If Clear, Hammer Down, Open Action", what must be fitted once the gun proves to be clear?
o: A cable lock through the action
questions.refText: If the gun proves to be clear, a chamber safety flag must be fitted. The action can remain open or be closed.

questions.q: What is the recommended physical (tap) signal sequence for a hearing-impaired competitor for "Are You Ready?", "Standby", and the Start Signal?
questions.refText: The recommended physical signals are taps on the competitor's weak side shoulder using a countdown protocol, namely 3 taps for "Are You Ready?", 2 taps for "Standby" and 1 tap to coincide with the Start Signal.

questions.q: Which of the following counts as "Movement" under Rule 8.5.1?
o: Taking more than one step in any direction, or changing shooting position
Adjusting an electronic sight while pointing at the ground
Aiming at a target from a fixed stance
questions.refText: "Movement" is defined as any of the actions below: Taking more than one step in any direction. Changing shooting position (e.g. from standing to kneeling, from seated to standing etc.).

questions.q: Assistance to a competitor during a course of fire is prohibited, except that a Range Officer assigned to a stage may:
o: Issue safety warnings to a competitor at any time
Reload the firearm for the competitor
Provide verbal coaching on target order
questions.refText: No assistance of any kind can be given to a competitor during a course of fire, except that any Range Officer assigned to a stage may issue safety warnings to a competitor at any time. Such warnings will not be grounds for the competitor to be awarded a reshoot.

questions.q: If any person appears downrange from the competitor during a course of fire, what happens to the course of fire?
o: It must immediately be terminated and the competitor required to reshoot
Only the affected target is rescored
questions.refText: In the event that any person appears downrange from the competitor during a course of fire, it must immediately be terminated and the competitor required to reshoot the course of fire.

questions.q: Drones or other remotely controlled devices at an IPSC match are:
o: Prohibited unless approved in advance by the Match Director
Permitted only at Level IV or higher matches
questions.refText: Drones or other remotely controlled devices are prohibited unless their use is approved in advance by the Match Director.

questions.q: Taking a sight picture and/or dry firing prior to the Start Signal is:
o: Prohibited, with a warning for the first occurrence and a procedural penalty for subsequent ones
Freely permitted at all times before the Start Signal
Grounds for immediate disqualification on the first occurrence
questions.refText: Competitors are prohibited from taking a sight picture and/or dry firing prior to the Start Signal. Violation will result in a warning for the first occurrence and one procedural penalty for each subsequent occurrence in the same match.

questions.q: During a walkthrough (course inspection), competitors are prohibited from using any sighting aid except:
questions.refText: Competitors are prohibited from using any sighting aid (e.g. the whole or part of an imitation or replica firearm, any part of a real firearm including any accessories thereof etc.), except for their own hands, while conducting their inspection ("walkthrough") of a course of fire.

questions.q: While scoring is in progress, how close may a competitor or delegate approach a target without Range Officer authorization?
questions.refText: Approaching Targets – While scoring is in progress, competitors or their delegate must not approach any target closer than 1 meter without the authorization of the Range Officer.

questions.q: If a target is prematurely patched or taped, preventing determination of the actual score, the Range Officer must:
o: Order the competitor to reshoot the course of fire
Score the target as a maximum hit
Score the target as a miss automatically
Ignore the error and continue scoring
questions.refText: Prematurely Patched Targets – If a target is prematurely patched or taped, preventing the determination of the actual score, the Range Officer must order the competitor to reshoot the course of fire.

questions.q: The scoring area of all IPSC scoring targets and no-shoots is deemed to be:
questions.refText: Impenetrable – The scoring area of all IPSC scoring targets and no-shoots is deemed to be impenetrable.

questions.q: If a slug or buckshot pellet strikes wholly within the scoring area of a paper target and continues on to strike down a scoring metal target, this is treated as:
o: Range equipment failure, requiring a reshoot after restoration
A normal double hit, both scored
A miss on the metal target only
questions.refText: Slug or a buckshot pellet strikes wholly within the scoring area of a paper target, and continues on to strike down a scoring metal target or no-shoot, this will be treated as range equipment failure (see Rule 4.7.1). The competitor will be required to reshoot the course of fire, after it has been restored.

questions.q: Props, walls, barriers, vision screens and other obstacles are deemed to be impenetrable:
questions.refText: Hard Cover – All props, walls, barriers, vision screens and other obstacles are deemed to be impenetrable "hard cover".

questions.q: Are target sticks considered Hard Cover?
o: No, target sticks are not Hard Cover
Only if painted a contrasting color
questions.refText: Target Sticks – Are not Hard Cover. Shots which have passed wholly or partially through target sticks and which hit a paper or metal target will count for score or penalty, as the case may be.

questions.q: Do hits from birdshot on a paper target count for score?
o: No, they will not count for score
Only if they strike the A zone
questions.refText: Birdshot Hits on Paper Targets – Hits from birdshot on a paper target will not count for score.

questions.q: What is the "Comstock" scoring method?
o: Unlimited time stops on the last shot, unlimited shots fired, a stipulated number of hits per target counts for score
A fixed par time with all shots scored equally
A method used only for Shoot-Offs
A method that scores only the single highest hit per target
questions.refText: "Comstock" – Unlimited time stops on the last shot, unlimited number of shots to be fired, stipulated number of hits per target to count for score.

questions.q: To how many decimal places are stage and match results calculated when ranking competitors?
o: No decimal places; whole numbers only
questions.refText: Stage results must rank competitors within the relevant Division in descending order of individual stage points achieved, calculated to 4 decimal places.

questions.q: How must ties in match results be broken?
o: The affected competitors shoot one or more courses of fire nominated by the Match Director; ties must never be broken by chance
By whichever competitor has the fewest procedural penalties overall
By comparing their scores on the very first stage of the match only
questions.refText: If, in the opinion of the Match Director, a tie in match results must be broken, the affected competitors must shoot one or more courses of fire, nominated or created by the Match Director, until the tie is broken...Ties must never be broken by chance.

questions.q: How many points do frangible targets usually score?
questions.refText: Scoring hits on IPSC targets will be scored in accordance with the values approved by the IPSC Assembly (see Appendices B and C and below). Frangible targets will usually score 5 points.

questions.q: The special scoring provisions for disappearing metal/frangible targets and difficult-shot targets (Rules 9.4.1.1-9.4.1.3) are restricted to what maximum percentage of the total number of targets in the match?
questions.refText: The scoring of targets as referred to in Rules 9.4.1.1, 9.4.1.2 and 9.4.1.3 is restricted to not more than 10% of the total number of targets in the match.

questions.q: Each hit visible on the scoring area of a paper no-shoot is penalized how many points, up to a maximum of how many hits per no-shoot?
o: Minus 10 points, up to a maximum of 2 hits
questions.refText: Each hit visible on the scoring area of a paper no-shoot will be penalized minus 10 points, up to a maximum of 2 hits per no-shoot.

questions.q: How many points is each miss penalized, except in the case of disappearing targets?
questions.refText: Each miss will be penalized minus 10 points, except in the case of disappearing targets (see Rule 9.9.2).

questions.q: For buckshot ammunition, how many hits per paper target count for score?
o: The single highest scoring hit only
The best two hits (the two highest scoring pellet strikes)
questions.refText: Scoring paper targets must be engaged with a minimum of one round each. In the case of slug ammunition 1 or 2 hits can be nominated to score (the default is 1 hit). In the case of buckshot ammunition the best two hits count for score i.e. the two highest scoring strikes of any pellets from any buckshot rounds fired.

questions.q: If the diameter of a hit from a slug or buckshot pellet touches the scoring line between two scoring areas, how is it scored?
o: It is scored the higher value
It is scored the lower value
It is not scored at all
It is scored as a miss
questions.refText: If the diameter of a hit from a slug or a buckshot pellet on a scoring paper target touches the scoring line between two scoring areas, or the line between the non-scoring border and a scoring area, or if it crosses multiple scoring areas, it will be scored the higher value.

questions.q: What is the minimum score for a stage?
o: There is no minimum; scores can go negative
questions.refText: The minimum score for a stage will be zero.

questions.q: A competitor who fails to engage the front of each scoring target with at least one round will incur:
o: One procedural penalty per target, plus appropriate penalties for misses
A zero score for the entire match
No penalty if the target array is completed
questions.refText: A competitor who fails to engage the front of each scoring target in a course of fire with at least one round will incur one procedural penalty per target for failure to engage the target, as well as appropriate penalties for misses (see Rule 10.2.7).

questions.q: For frangible targets to count for score, they must:
o: Be fully penetrated or break with a piece separated from the original target
Simply be struck anywhere by the shot pattern
Be hit by at least two pellets
questions.refText: Frangible targets must be fully penetrated or break with a piece separated from the original target to be counted for score.

questions.q: If a wad causes an extra hole in a paper target and it cannot be determined which hole was caused by the actual slug, what happens?
o: The competitor must reshoot the stage
The extra hole is simply ignored
The Range Master decides by coin flip
questions.refText: If a wad has caused an extra hole in a paper target and it cannot be determined which hole has been caused by the actual slug, the competitor must reshoot the stage.

questions.q: A competitor who fails to verify a target during the scoring process:
o: Loses all right of appeal in respect of scoring that target
Automatically receives the benefit of the doubt on any dispute
questions.refText: A competitor (or his delegate) who fails to verify a target during the scoring process loses all right of appeal in respect of scoring that target.

questions.q: A challenge to a score or penalty must be appealed to the Range Officer:
o: Prior to the subject target being painted, patched, or reset
Within 24 hours of the match ending
Only after the entire match is complete
Within 1 hour of the results being posted
questions.refText: Any challenge to a score or penalty must be appealed to the Range Officer by the competitor (or his delegate) prior to the subject target being painted, patched, or reset, failing which such challenges will not be accepted.

questions.q: The Range Master's ruling in respect of the scoring of hits on targets and no-shoots is:
o: Final; no further appeals are permitted with respect to such scoring decisions
Subject to appeal to the Arbitration Committee
Only binding for that stage, not the whole match
questions.refText: The Range Master's ruling in respect of the scoring of hits on targets and no-shoots will be final. No further appeals are permitted with respect to such scoring decisions.

questions.q: On the score sheet, how must scores, penalties, and elapsed time be recorded?
o: Whole numbers for scores/penalties; elapsed time to 2 decimal places
Whole numbers for everything, including time
questions.refText: Whole numbers should be used to record all scores or penalties. The elapsed time taken by the competitor to complete the course of fire must be recorded to 2 decimal places in the appropriate place.

questions.q: A score sheet signed by both a competitor and a Range Officer is considered:
o: Conclusive evidence that the course of fire has been completed, scored and recorded accurately
Merely a provisional record subject to revision at any time
Void if either party later disagrees
Valid only until the next stage begins
questions.refText: A score sheet signed by both a competitor and a Range Officer is conclusive evidence that the course of fire has been completed, and that the time, scores and penalties recorded on the score sheet, are accurate and uncontested.

questions.q: If a reshoot is not possible and the time is missing from the score sheet, what score does the competitor receive for the stage?
o: The highest recorded score of the field
The score is simply omitted from match totals
questions.refText: In the event that a reshoot is not possible for any reason, the following actions will prevail: If the time is missing, the competitor will receive a zero score for the stage.

questions.q: If a competitor detects an error in the provisional stage results, within what time limit must an appeal be filed with the Stats Officer?
o: 1 hour after the results were actually posted
questions.refText: If a competitor detects an error in those results, he must file an appeal with the Stats Officer within 1 hour after the results were actually posted. If the appeal is not filed within the time limit, the posted scores will stand and the appeal will be dismissed.

questions.q: Which of the following moving-target scenarios is considered NOT disappearing, and will always incur failure-to-engage or miss penalties?
o: Targets that present at least a portion of the A zone when at rest, before or after activation
Targets engageable only for part of an apparatus's travel and not re-engageable
Targets that never present the A zone at rest
Targets activated by a mechanical lever
questions.refText: Moving targets which present at least a portion of the A zone when at rest (either before or after initial activation), or which continuously appear and disappear for the duration of a competitor's attempt at a COF, are not disappearing and will always incur failure to engage and/or miss penalties.

questions.q: Only what device may be used to record the official elapsed time of a competitor's attempt at a course of fire?
o: The timing device operated by a Range Officer
questions.refText: Only the timing device operated by a Range Officer must be used to record the official elapsed time of a competitor's attempt at a course of fire.

questions.q: For Level IV or higher matches, which scoring programs are the official ones (unless another is approved by the IPSC President)?
o: The latest versions of WinMSS and the IPSC ESS
questions.refText: The official scoring programs for all Level IV or higher matches are the latest versions of the Windows® Match Scoring System (WinMSS) and the IPSC ESS, unless another scoring program is approved by the IPSC President.

questions.q: How many points is each procedural penalty assessed?
questions.refText: Procedural penalties are assessed at minus 10 points each.

questions.q: Can procedural penalties be nullified by further competitor action (e.g. shooting the target again correctly)?
o: No, procedural penalties cannot be nullified by further competitor action
Only if the Range Officer agrees
Only for the first offense in a match
questions.refText: Procedural penalties cannot be nullified by further competitor action. For example, a competitor who fires a shot at a target while faulting a line will still incur the applicable penalties even though he subsequently shoots at the same target while not faulting the line.

questions.q: A competitor who fires shots while any part of their body is touching the ground or an object beyond a Fault Line normally receives what penalty?
o: 1 procedural penalty per shot fired, always
No penalty unless a target is missed
questions.refText: A competitor who fires shots while any part of their body is touching the ground or any object beyond a Fault Line will receive 1 procedural penalty for each occurrence. No penalty is assessed if a competitor does not fire any shots while faulting except when Rule 2.2.1.5 applies.

questions.q: A competitor who fails to comply with a mandatory reload incurs what penalty?
o: 1 procedural penalty for each shot fired after the point where the reload was required until a reload is performed
A single fixed penalty of 10 points regardless of shots fired
Loss of the stage's highest scoring hit
questions.refText: A competitor who fails to comply with a mandatory reload will incur 1 procedural penalty for each shot fired after the point where the reload was required until a reload is performed.

questions.q: In a Cooper Tunnel, a competitor who disturbs overhead material receives what penalty, unless caused by muzzle gases or recoil?
o: 1 procedural penalty for each piece of overhead material which falls
A single fixed penalty regardless of pieces
No penalty; Cooper Tunnels are never penalized
questions.refText: In a Cooper Tunnel, a competitor who disturbs one or more pieces of the overhead material will receive 1 procedural penalty for each piece of overhead material which falls. Overhead material which falls as a result of the competitor bumping or striking the uprights, or as a result of muzzle gases or recoil, will not be penalized.

questions.q: A competitor who is "creeping" or moving to a more advantageous position after "Standby" but before the Start Signal incurs:
o: 1 procedural penalty (or a warning and restart if the RO stops him in time)
A zero score for the stage
No penalty as long as he does not fire
questions.refText: A competitor who is creeping...or physically moving to a more advantageous shooting position or stance after the "Standby" command and prior to issuance of the Start Signal, will incur 1 procedural penalty. If the Range Officer can stop the competitor in time, a warning will be issued for the first offense and the competitor will be restarted.

questions.q: A special penalty for a competitor unable to fully execute part of a course of fire due to incapacity or injury may range from what percentage of points "as shot"?
questions.refText: If the request is approved by the Range Master, he must state, in advance of the competitor attempting the course of fire, the extent of the special penalty, ranging from 1% to 20% of the competitor's points "as shot", to be deducted.

questions.q: A competitor who fires shots over a barrier constructed to a height of at least 1.8 meters incurs:
o: 1 procedural penalty for each shot fired
A single fixed penalty regardless of shots fired
No penalty as long as the target is hit
questions.refText: A competitor who fires shots over a barrier constructed to a height of at least 1.8 meters will incur 1 procedural penalty for each shot fired (also see Rule 2.2.3.1).

questions.q: A competitor who commits a safety infraction during an IPSC match will be:
o: Disqualified and prohibited from attempting any remaining courses of fire, pending any appeal
Given a single large procedural penalty
questions.refText: A competitor who commits a safety infraction or any other prohibited activity during an IPSC match will be disqualified, and will be prohibited from attempting any remaining courses of fire regardless of the schedule or physical layout of the match, pending the verdict of any appeal.

questions.q: A shot that strikes the ground within how many meters of the competitor (with certain exceptions) is an accidental discharge?
questions.refText: A shot which strikes the ground within 3 meters of the competitor, except when shooting at a paper or frangible target closer than 3 meters to the competitor. A shot which strikes the ground within 3 meters of the competitor due to a "squib" load is exempt from this rule.

questions.q: A shot fired at a metal target from a distance closer than the applicable minimum distance is treated as an accidental discharge. What is that minimum distance for slug ammunition?
questions.refText: A shot fired at a metal target from a distance of less than 5 meters when using birdshot or buckshot ammunition or 40 meters when using slug ammunition. The distance is measured from the front of the target to the nearest part of the competitor's body in contact with the ground.

questions.q: If it is established that a discharge was caused by a broken or defective part of the firearm, what is the outcome?
o: No disqualification is invoked, but the competitor's scores for that stage will be zero
The competitor receives a full reshoot with no penalty
The competitor is only warned, with the stage scored as shot
questions.refText: In this Section, if it can be established that the cause of the discharge is due to a broken or defective part of the firearm, the competitor has not committed any safety infraction in this Section, and a disqualification will not be invoked, but the competitor's scores for that stage will be zero.

questions.q: Handling a firearm at any time except in a designated Safety Area, or elsewhere deemed safe by / under direct command of a Range Officer, may invoke:
o: A warning only for the first occurrence
No consequence if the firearm is unloaded
questions.refText: Handling a firearm at any time except when in a designated Safety Area, or elsewhere deemed safe by a Range Officer, or when under the supervision of, and in response to a direct command issued by, a Range Officer may invoke a disqualification.

questions.q: When fitting the chamber safety flag in compliance with Rule 8.3.7.2, the muzzle may point uprange within what radius of the competitor's feet as an exception to Rule 10.5.2?
questions.refText: Allowing the muzzle of a firearm to point uprange, or past the default, or specific safe angles of fire during a course of fire. Exception: when fitting the chamber safety flag in compliance with Rule 8.3.7.2 the muzzle may point uprange within a radius of 50 cm from a competitor's feet.

questions.q: "Sweeping" refers to:
o: Allowing the muzzle of a shotgun to point at any part of the competitor's own body during a course of fire
Clearing spent shells from the ground after a stage
Moving through a course of fire without stopping
questions.refText: Allowing the muzzle of a shotgun to point at any part of the competitor's body during a course of fire (i.e. sweeping).

questions.q: Using more than one firearm during a course of fire results in:
o: A warning for the first offense only
No penalty if only one is ever fired
questions.refText: Using more than one firearm during a course of fire. [Examples of unsafe gun handling resulting in disqualification] (see Rule 5.1.9).

questions.q: A competitor who retrieves his own dropped firearm during a course of fire will receive:
o: No penalty if the firearm is unloaded
A warning for the first occurrence
questions.refText: Retrieving a dropped firearm. Dropped firearms must always be retrieved by a Range Officer who will, after checking and/or clearing the firearm, return it to the competitor in a safe condition...a competitor who retrieves a dropped firearm will receive a disqualification.

questions.q: A competitor deemed by a Range Officer to have intentionally removed eye or ear protection to gain a reshoot or advantage will be:
o: Required to reshoot with no penalty
questions.refText: A competitor who is deemed by a Range Officer to have intentionally removed or caused the loss of eye or ear protection in order to gain a reshoot or advantage will be disqualified.

questions.q: Persons visibly under the influence of alcohol or prohibited drugs at an IPSC match, in the opinion of the Range Master, will be:
o: Disqualified from the match and may be required to leave the range
Assessed a procedural penalty per occurrence
Only reported to their Regional Director
questions.refText: Except when used for medicinal purposes, competitors and officials at matches must not be affected by drugs (including alcohol) of any sort during matches. Any person, who in the opinion of the Range Master is visibly under the influence of any of the items described herein, will be disqualified from the match and may be required to leave the range.

questions.q: Appeals arising from a disqualification for a safety infraction will only be accepted to determine:
o: Whether exceptional circumstances warrant reconsideration of the disqualification
Whether the competitor's overall match placing should change
Whether the Range Officer was certified
Whether the penalty amount was calculated correctly
questions.refText: Appeals arising from a disqualification for a safety infraction will only be accepted to determine whether exceptional circumstances warrant reconsideration of the disqualification. However, the commission of the infraction as described by the Match Official is not subject to challenge or appeal.

questions.q: What is the initial chain of appeal for a disputed call at a stage?
o: Range Officer, then Chief Range Officer, then Range Master
Match Director, then Range Master, then Range Officer
questions.refText: Appeals – The Range Officer makes decisions initially. If the appellant disagrees with a decision, the Chief Range Officer for the stage or area in question should be asked to rule. If a disagreement still exists, the Range Master must be asked to rule.

questions.q: If a competitor continues to disagree after the Range Master's ruling, he may appeal to the Arbitration Committee by submitting:
o: A petition signed by other competitors
A request directly to the IPSC President
questions.refText: Appeal to Committee – Should the appellant continue to disagree with the decision he may appeal to the Arbitration Committee by submitting a first party appeal.

questions.q: At Level III or higher matches, who serves as Chairman of the Arbitration Committee (with no vote)?
o: The IPSC President, his delegate, or a certified Match Official appointed by the Match Director, in that order
The senior Match Official present, regardless of role
questions.refText: The IPSC President, or his delegate, or a certified Match Official appointed by the Match Director, (in that order) will serve as Chairman of the committee with no vote.

questions.q: At Level III or higher matches, how many arbitrators are appointed to the Arbitration Committee, each with one vote?
questions.refText: Three arbitrators will be appointed by the IPSC President, or his delegate, or by the Match Director, (in that order), with one vote each.

questions.q: At Level I and II matches, who appoints the Arbitration Committee and how many committee members are there?
o: The Match Director appoints three experienced persons who are not parties to the appeal
The Range Master appoints five certified officials
The IPSC Executive Council appoints one arbitrator
Competitors vote to select the committee
questions.refText: Level I and II Matches – The Match Director can appoint an Arbitration Committee of three experienced persons who are not parties to the appeal and who do not have a direct conflict of interest in the outcome of the appeal.
