questions.q: Within what time limit must a written appeal to arbitration be submitted to the Range Master, along with the applicable fee?
questions.refText: Time Limit for Appeal to Arbitration – Written appeals to arbitration must be submitted to the Range Master on the appropriate form, accompanied by the applicable fee, within one hour of the time of the disputed call as recorded by Match Officials.

questions.q: Within what time limit must the Arbitration Committee reach a decision (or before results are declared final, whichever is first)?
questions.refText: Decision Time Limit – The Committee must reach a decision within 24 hours of the request for arbitration or before the results have been declared final by the Match Director, whichever comes first. If the Committee fails to render a decision within the prescribed period, both a first and third party appellant will automatically succeed in their appeal, and the fee will be returned.

questions.q: For Level III or higher matches, what is the appeal fee to arbitration?
o: US$100.00 or the equivalent of the maximum individual match entry fee, whichever is lower
There is no fee at Level III or higher
questions.refText: Amount – For Level III or higher matches, the appeal fee to enable an appellant to appeal to arbitration will be US$100.00 or the equivalent of the maximum individual match entry fee (whichever is lower), in local currency.

questions.q: How does the Arbitration Committee reach its decision during deliberation?
o: By a public show of hands at the range
questions.refText: Deliberation – When the Committee is satisfied that they are in possession of all information and evidence relevant to the appeal, they will deliberate privately and will reach their decision by majority vote.

questions.q: The decision of the Arbitration Committee is final and may not be appealed unless:
o: New evidence received after the decision, but before results are declared final, warrants reconsideration
The losing party requests a second hearing within 24 hours
questions.refText: Decision is Final – The decision of the Committee is final and may not be appealed unless, in the opinion of the Range Master, new evidence received after the decision, but before the results have been declared final by the Match Director, warrants reconsideration.

questions.q: Decisions of the Arbitration Committee are recorded and will:
o: Provide precedent for any similar and subsequent incident during that match
Have no bearing on future incidents
Only apply to the specific competitor involved
questions.refText: Minutes – Decisions of the Arbitration Committee will be recorded and will provide precedent for any similar and subsequent incident during that match.

questions.q: Who is responsible for the interpretation of the IPSC rules and regulations?
o: The Match Director of each match
questions.refText: Interpretation of these rules and regulations is the responsibility of the IPSC Executive Council.

questions.q: Rule interpretations published on the IPSC website become precedent and apply to matches commencing how many days after publication?
questions.refText: All rule interpretations published on the IPSC website will be deemed to be precedents and will be applied to all IPSC sanctioned matches commencing on or after 7 days from the date of publication.

questions.q: If there are discrepancies between the English version of the IPSC Rules and a translated version, which prevails?
o: The translated version used at the host match
Whichever version the Match Director prefers
The most recently published version regardless of language
questions.refText: English is the official language of the IPSC Rules. Should there be discrepancies between the English language version of these rules and versions presented in other languages, the English language version will prevail.

questions.q: How does the rulebook treat references to the male gender ("he", "his", "him")?
o: They are deemed to include the female gender
They apply only to male competitors
They must be interpreted case-by-case by the Range Master
They are considered errors to be corrected
questions.refText: References made herein to the male gender (i.e. "he", "his", "him") are deemed to include the female gender (i.e. "she", "her").

questions.q: Throughout the rules, where measurements are expressed, what is the status of the figures shown in brackets?
o: They are provided only as a guide
They are the legally binding value, overriding the primary figure
They apply only outside the host country
They must be used for chronograph testing only
questions.refText: Measurements – Throughout these rules, where measurements are expressed, those in brackets are only provided as a guide.

questions.q: In the Glossary, what does "Aftermarket" mean?
o: Items not manufactured by the OFM, and/or bearing identifying marks of a different OFM
Any item purchased after the match has started
A firearm modification made without Range Master approval
Equipment purchased from an official match vendor
questions.refText: Aftermarket – Items not manufactured by the OFM, and/or bearing identifying marks of a different OFM.

questions.q: How is "Attempt at (COF)" defined in the Glossary?
o: The period from issuance of the Start Signal to when the competitor indicates he has finished shooting
The period from "Load and Make Ready" until the walkthrough ends
Any single shot fired at a target
The total duration of a competitor's participation in a match
questions.refText: Attempt at (COF) – The period from issuance of the Start Signal to when the competitor indicates that he has finished shooting, in response to Rule 8.3.6.

questions.q: What is a "Berm" as defined in the Glossary?
o: A raised structure of sand, soil or other materials used to contain bullets and/or separate shooting bays
A type of metal no-shoot target
A safety flag fitted to a long gun
questions.refText: Berm – A raised structure of sand, soil or other materials used to contain bullets and/or to separate one shooting bay and/or COF from another.

questions.q: What defines a "Chamber Safety Flag" in the Glossary?
o: A brightly colored device, incapable of insertion into a loaded chamber, with an integral tab or ribbon protruding from the firearm
Any object placed in the ejection port
A padlock through the trigger guard
A red flag placed on the ground beside the firing line
questions.refText: Chamber Safety Flag – A brightly colored device, no part of which resembles a round or any part thereof. The flag must be incapable of being inserted into a firearm which has a loaded chamber and must, while fitted, prevent a round from being inserted into the chamber. The flag must have an integral tab or ribbon clearly protruding from the firearm.

questions.q: What is a "Detonation" as defined in the Glossary?
o: Ignition of the primer, other than by action of a firing pin, where the shot/slug and/or wad does not pass through the barrel
Any shot fired during a course of fire
The explosion of a squib load inside the barrel
The failure of a cartridge to ignite at all
questions.refText: Detonation – Ignition of the primer, other than by action of a firing pin, where the shot or a slug and/or the wad does not pass through the barrel of a firearm (e.g. when the action of a firearm is being manually retracted, when a round is dropped).

questions.q: What is meant by "Downrange" in the Glossary?
o: The general area where the muzzle may be safely pointed during a COF and/or where bullets are likely to impact
Any area behind the firing line
The area where spectators are permitted to stand
The area within a Safety Area
questions.refText: Downrange – The general area of a stage, shooting bay or range, where the muzzle of a firearm may be safely pointed during a course of fire and/or where bullets are intended or are likely to impact.

questions.q: How is "Dry firing" defined in the Glossary?
o: The activation of the trigger and/or action of a firearm totally devoid of ammunition
Firing a shot at a target without hitting it
Testing a firearm for malfunctions before a match
questions.refText: Dry firing – The activation of the trigger and/or action of a firearm which is totally devoid of ammunition.

questions.q: According to the Glossary, what is "Engage"?
o: Firing a shot at a target; firing a shot at, but missing, a target is not a "failure to engage"
Successfully hitting a target with every round fired
Loading a firearm during a course of fire
Approaching a target to score it
questions.refText: Engage – Firing a shot at a target. Firing a shot at, but missing, a target is not a "failure to engage". The malfunction of a firearm or a round which prevents a shot being fired, is deemed to be a "failure to engage".

questions.q: What is a "False start" as defined in the Glossary?
o: Beginning an attempt at a COF prior to the Start Signal
Failing to react to the Start Signal at all
Arriving late for a scheduled squad
Any procedural penalty incurred before shooting begins
questions.refText: False start – Beginning an attempt at a COF prior to the Start Signal (see Rule 8.3.4).

questions.q: What defines a "Frangible target" in the Glossary?
o: A target, such as a clay pigeon or tile, capable of being easily broken into two or more pieces when hit
Any paper target with a non-scoring border
A metal target coated with reactive paint
questions.refText: Frangible target – A target, such as a clay pigeon or tile, capable of being easily broken into two or more pieces when hit.

questions.q: According to the Glossary, how many grains are in one ounce (used to calculate power factor)?
questions.refText: Grain – A unit of measurement used to calculate a power factor (437.5 grains per ounce, 15.432 grains per gram, 1 grain = 0.0648 grams).

questions.q: According to the Glossary, when is a firearm considered "Loaded"?
o: When it has a live or dummy round in the chamber/cylinder or in an inserted/fitted magazine
Only when a live round is chambered
Only when the safety catch is off
Only when the hammer is cocked
questions.refText: Loaded – A firearm having a live or dummy round in the chamber or cylinder, or having a live or dummy round in an inserted or fitted magazine(s).

questions.q: In the Glossary, what is the defined meaning of the word "May"?
questions.refText: May – Entirely optional.

questions.q: In the Glossary, what is the defined meaning of the word "Must"?
o: Recommended for Level III and above only
questions.refText: Must – Mandatory.

questions.q: In the Glossary, what is the defined meaning of the word "Should"?
o: Prohibited except by Range Master waiver
questions.refText: Should – Optional but highly recommended.

questions.q: According to the Glossary, what is a "Prototype" firearm?
o: A firearm in a configuration not in mass production and/or not available to the general public
A firearm produced by a factory in fewer than 1000 units
A firearm modified after purchase by a gunsmith
questions.refText: Prototype – A firearm in a configuration which is not in mass production and/or is not available to the general public.

questions.q: What is a "Reshoot" as defined in the Glossary?
o: A competitor's subsequent attempt at a COF, authorized in advance by a Range Officer or Arbitration Committee
Any second shot fired at the same target
A stage that is deleted from match results
A competitor's first attempt after a false start
questions.refText: Reshoot – A competitor's subsequent attempt at a course of fire, authorized in advance by a Range Officer or an Arbitration Committee.

questions.q: What is a "Squib Load" as defined in the Glossary?
o: A defective cartridge resulting in one or more projectiles and/or the wad failing to exit the barrel, or exiting at extremely low velocity
A cartridge with excessive powder charge
A blank round used for demonstrations
A cartridge that fails to fire at all
questions.refText: Squib Load – A defective cartridge resulting in one or more projectiles and/or the wad failing to exit the barrel, or exiting the barrel at extremely low velocity.

questions.q: What does "Sweeping" mean in the Glossary?
o: Pointing the muzzle at any part of the competitor's own body when a handgun is not securely holstered or a long gun's chamber flag is not inserted
Clearing debris from the shooting area before a course of fire
Moving through a course of fire quickly
Checking a firearm is clear at the safety table
questions.refText: Sweeping – Pointing the muzzle of a firearm at any part of the competitor's body during a course of fire when a handgun is held or touched while not securely holstered, or when a long gun is held while a chamber safety flag is not inserted (see Rule 10.5.5).

questions.q: What is a "Target Array" as defined in the Glossary?
o: A collection of approved targets that can only be seen from any single location or view
Any group of five or more targets
A set of targets used exclusively in Classifiers
The complete set of targets used throughout a match
questions.refText: Target Array – A collection of approved targets that can only be seen from any single location or view.

questions.q: What distinguishes conventional wads from specialized long-range wads in the Glossary?
o: Conventional wads have slits and open/separate from the pellets immediately on exiting the barrel; long-range wads encapsulate and hold the pellets together after exiting
Conventional wads are made of plastic, long-range wads are always fiber
There is no functional difference between them
Long-range wads are used only with slugs
questions.refText: Wads (Conventional) – Fiber wads or plastic wads designed to start opening and separating from the pellets immediately on exiting the barrel...Wads (Specialized Long-range) – Wads designed to encapsulate and/or surround the pellets and after exiting the barrel remain in place during the early part of the flight to hold the pellets together.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, what is the recommended minimum number of rounds for a Level I Shotgun match?
questions.refText: Recommended minimum rounds - Shotgun: Level I 40, Level II 80, Level III 150, Level IV 200, Level V 250.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, what is the recommended minimum number of rounds for a Level V Shotgun match?
questions.refText: Recommended minimum rounds - Shotgun: Level I 40, Level II 80, Level III 150, Level IV 200, Level V 250.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, what is the recommended minimum number of stages for a Level IV Shotgun match?
questions.refText: Recommended minimum stages - Shotgun: Level I 3, Level II 6, Level III 12, Level IV 24, Level V 30.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, at which match level does a Chronograph first become mandatory ('M')?
questions.refText: 15. Chronograph — Level II: R (Recommended), Level III: R, Level IV: M (Mandatory), Level V: M.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, one Range Master approved by the IPSC Executive Council is mandatory starting at which level?
questions.refText: 6. Range Master approved by IPSC Executive Council — Mandatory (M) at Level IV and Level V.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, international sanctioning of Level I and Level II matches is:
o: Not required; each Regional Director may set his own criteria for sanctioning them
Mandatory through the IPSC Executive Council
Handled exclusively by the International Range Officers Association
questions.refText: 24. International sanctioning of Level I and Level II matches is not required. However, each Regional Director is entitled to establish his own criteria and procedures for sanctioning of such matches held within his own Region.

questions.q: According to Appendix A1, what match rating (points) is assigned to a Level III match?
questions.refText: 23. Match rating (points) — Level I: 1, Level II: 2, Level III: 3, Level IV: 4, Level V: 5.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, what is the mandatory minimum number of competitors per Division at a Level III match for it to be recognized?
questions.refText: 1. Divisions: Level I & II – A minimum of 5 competitors per Division (recommended). Level III – A minimum of 10 competitors per Division (mandatory). Level IV & V – A minimum of 20 competitors per Division (mandatory).

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, what is the mandatory minimum number of competitors per Division at Level IV and V matches?
questions.refText: 1. Divisions: ...Level IV & V – A minimum of 20 competitors per Division (mandatory).

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, what is the minimum number of competitors per Division Category, at all match levels, for the Category to be recognized?
questions.refText: 2. Categories: ...All level matches – A minimum of 5 competitors per Division Category (see approved list below).

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, at what age (until 31st December of the year they reach it) does a competitor qualify as "Senior"?
questions.refText: (h) Senior – Competitors who are over the age of 50 on the first day of the match.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, at what age does a competitor qualify as "Super Senior"?
questions.refText: (j) Super Senior – Competitors who are over the age of 60 on the first day of the match.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, at what age does a competitor qualify as "Grand Senior"?
questions.refText: (k) Grand Senior – Competitors who are over the age of 70 on the first day of the match.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, a "Junior" competitor is under what age (until the 31st December of the year they reach it)?
questions.refText: (f) Junior – Competitors who are under the age of 21 until the 31st December of the year in which they become 21 years of age.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, a "Grand Junior" competitor is under what age (until the 31st December of the year they reach it)?
questions.refText: (b) Grand Junior – Competitors who are under the age of 14 until the 31st December of the year in which they become 14 years of age.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, a "Super Junior" competitor is under what age (until the 31st December of the year they reach it)?
questions.refText: (d) Super Junior – Competitors who are under the age of 18 until the 31st December of the year in which they become 18 years of age.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, a Family Team consists of two members, one being a Junior/Senior-age relative and the other being:
o: Either a parent or grandparent of that Junior-category member
Any two competitors of the same age category
Two competitors of the same gender only
Any two members of the same Regional Team
questions.refText: (m) Teams by Family. Family Teams consist of two members, one being either a Grand Junior, Lady Grand Junior, Super Junior, Lady Super Junior, Junior or Lady Junior and the other either a parent or grandparent of the Grand Junior, Lady Grand Junior, Super Junior, Lady Super Junior, Junior or Lady Junior.

questions.q: According to Appendix A2, IPSC Level IV & V matches must recognize Team Categories for team awards when a minimum of how many teams are registered in the Category?
questions.refText: 4. Team Categories: IPSC Level IV & V matches must recognize any of the following Team Categories for team awards when a minimum of 3 teams are registered in the Category.

questions.q: According to the Approved Stage Ratios table (Appendix A4), for a 20-stage match, which of the following is a listed approved Short/Medium/Long combination?
questions.refText: Approved Stage Ratios table: for 20 stages, listed combinations include 10 Short / 7 Medium / 3 Long (also 11/6/3 and 9/8/3).

questions.q: On the IPSC Target, IPSC Mini Target and IPSC Universal Target scoring diagrams, how many points is the A zone worth?
questions.refText: Scoring Zone A = 5, C = 4, D = 2 (IPSC Target, IPSC Mini Target and IPSC Universal Target).

questions.q: On the IPSC Target, IPSC Mini Target and IPSC Universal Target scoring diagrams, how many points is the D zone worth?
questions.refText: Scoring Zone A = 5, C = 4, D = 2 (IPSC Target, IPSC Mini Target and IPSC Universal Target).

questions.q: According to Appendix C1, what caliber and configuration is specified for the test gun used in target calibration?
o: 12 gauge, maximum barrel length 66 cm, true cylinder or open choked barrel, any action type
20 gauge, maximum barrel length 50 cm, full choke only
12 gauge pump-action only, no barrel length limit
Any gauge, provided it matches the Division being tested
questions.refText: Test Gun Specification: Caliber: 12 gauge. Maximum barrel length – 66 cms. True cylinder or open choked barrel. Any action type.

questions.q: According to Appendix C1, all ammunition used in a match is required to conform to a minimum power factor of:
questions.refText: All ammunition used in a match is required to conform to a minimum PF of 480 and it is the competitor's responsibility to choose appropriate cartridges.

questions.q: According to Appendix C1's test cartridge specifications for Birdshot Courses of Fire, what is the maximum total weight of shot (pellets) permitted?
questions.refText: For Birdshot Courses of Fire...Maximum total weight of shot (pellets): 28.3 grams (1 ounce). The manufacturer's stated velocity is to be less than 1300 fps. (This equates to a maximum PF of 568).

questions.q: According to Appendix C1's test cartridge specifications for Buckshot Courses of Fire, what is the maximum number of pellets per cartridge?
questions.refText: For Buckshot Courses of Fire: Buckshot: OO or local equivalent. Max of 9 pellets per cartridge.

questions.q: According to Appendix C1's test cartridge specifications for Slug Courses of Fire, what is the maximum permitted power factor as calculated from manufacturer's stated data?
questions.refText: For Slug Courses of Fire: Max weight of slug 28.3 grams (1 ounce). Maximum power factor to be less than 590 as calculated from manufacturer's stated data. (A PF of around 520 or less is preferred).

questions.q: According to Appendix C1, what is the maximum number of times a competitor may request a metal target be tested during a match of up to (and including) 15 stages?
questions.refText: A competitor is permitted a maximum of 3 requests for testing during a match of up to (and including) 15 stages and to a maximum of 4 requests for testing during a match of over 15 stages.

questions.q: According to Appendix C1, if a popper falls for a reason other than a proper hit (e.g. wind action) before it can be calibrated, what must happen?
o: The target is simply scored as a miss
No action is taken; the course continues as shot
questions.refText: If the popper falls for any other reason (e.g. wind action), before it can be calibrated, a reshoot must be ordered.

questions.q: According to Appendix C2, how many points can an IPSC Popper score in Rifle/Shotgun matches?
questions.refText: IPSC Poppers - RIFLE / SHOTGUN Scoring: 5 or 10 points (Rules 9.4.1.1 & 9.4.1.2). Penalty for Miss/No-Shoot: Minus 10 points.

questions.q: According to Appendix C2, what is the tolerance for the calibration zone marking on an IPSC Popper?
questions.refText: Tolerance +/- 0.5 cm (IPSC Poppers calibration zone).

questions.q: According to Appendix C3, what are the minimum and maximum diameters for a round IPSC Metal Plate used in Rifle/Shotgun matches?
questions.refText: Dimensions - Round: Rifle/Shotgun Minimum 15 cm Ø, Maximum 30 cm Ø.

questions.q: According to Appendix C3, using metal plates that can accidentally turn edge-on or sideways when hit may result in:
o: A warning to the Range Master only
A mandatory reshoot for all affected competitors
questions.refText: Metal plates which can accidentally turn edge-on or sideways when hit are expressly prohibited. Using them may result in the withdrawal of IPSC sanction (see Rule 4.3.1.1).

questions.q: According to Appendix D, what is the minimum power factor required across all Shotgun Divisions?
questions.refText: 1. Minimum Power Factor — 480 (all Shotgun Divisions).

questions.q: According to Appendix D, which Shotgun Divisions permit optical or electronic sights?
o: SG Standard and SG Standard Manual only
questions.refText: 9. Optical or Electronic sights — SG Open: Yes, SG Modified: Yes, SG Standard: No, SG Standard Manual: No.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, in which Shotgun Divisions are prototypes permitted?
o: SG Standard and SG Standard Manual
questions.refText: 4. Prototypes permitted — SG Open: Yes, SG Modified: Yes, SG Standard: No, SG Standard Manual: No.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, what is the maximum overall length permitted for an SG Open or SG Modified gun (fitted with longest magazine)?
questions.refText: 6. Maximum overall length for gun — SG Open/SG Modified: 1320 mm, see Point 17. The internal length of the box is 1320 mm (tolerance: +1 mm, -0 mm).

questions.q: According to Appendix D, in SG Open Division, detachable magazines or tubes accessible during a COF must not contain more than how many rounds at the Start Signal?
questions.refText: 18. Detachable magazines or tubes accessible to a competitor during a COF must not contain more than 10 rounds at the Start Signal. However, detachable magazines with an original maximum capacity of up to 12 rounds are permitted.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, guns with fixed magazines in SG Open Division may have an initial load of how many rounds?
questions.refText: 18. ...Guns with fixed magazines may have an initial load of 14 rounds.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, what is the maximum initial load capacity restriction for SG Standard and SG Standard Manual Divisions?
questions.refText: 12. Capacity restrictions for initial load prior to the Start Signal — SG Modified: Max. of 14 rounds loaded, SG Standard: Max. of 9 rounds loaded, SG Standard Manual: Max. of 9 rounds loaded.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, which Division permits speed loaders, and what is their maximum capacity?
questions.refText: 14. Speed loaders — SG Open: Yes – 6 rounds maximum. SG Modified/SG Standard/SG Standard Manual: No.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, which Divisions permit detachable magazines?
questions.refText: 13. Detachable magazines — SG Open: Yes, see Point 18. SG Modified/SG Standard/SG Standard Manual: No.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, an SG Standard Manual Division shotgun must have what type of action, requiring the competitor to physically extract and load each round?
o: Any complete manual action (pump, slide, break-open, lever, bolt action)
questions.refText: 22. Any complete manual action shotgun (i.e. pump action, slide action, break-open, lever action, bolt action) produced by a factory and available to the general public, where extraction of a spent case and loading of a new round are caused entirely by a competitor's physical manipulation.

questions.q: According to Appendix D, modifications or attachments to the loading floor plate in SG Modified Division must not exceed what length or protrude more than what distance?
o: Not exceed 75 mm in length, not protrude more than 32 mm
Not exceed 50 mm in length, not protrude more than 20 mm
Not exceed 100 mm in length, not protrude more than 40 mm
There is no limit in SG Modified Division
questions.refText: 19. Modifications or attachments can be made or added to the loading floor plate to facilitate easier loading. Such modifications or attachments must not exceed 75 mm in length and must not protrude more than 32 mm from the standard frame of the shotgun in any direction.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, what is the minimum caliber for shotgun ammunition specified in the general table?
questions.refText: General - 3. Minimum caliber: 20 gauge / 20 bore.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, are home-loaded (hand-loaded) shotgun cartridges acceptable, or is factory-produced ammunition required?
o: Home loads are acceptable; factory-produced ammunition is not exclusively required
Home loads are acceptable only in SG Open Division
Home loads require Regional Director approval for every match
questions.refText: 5. Factory produced ammunition only — No. Home loads are acceptable.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, steel and tungsten based shot are permitted for use against which target types only?
o: Paper, frangible and synthetic targets only
No target types; they are prohibited entirely
questions.refText: 8. Tungsten Based shot — Permitted for paper, frangible and synthetic targets only. 9. Steel shot — Permitted for paper, frangible and synthetic targets only.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, at Level III matches and above, what is the maximum combined number of rounds required for buckshot and slug ammunition?
questions.refText: 19. At Level III matches and above the maximum required number of rounds for buckshot and slug ammunition (combined) is restricted to 80 rounds.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, what shot diameter range defines acceptable Birdshot sizes?
questions.refText: Acceptable Birdshot Sizes: Shot diameters of 3.5 mm to 2.0 mm (.138 inches to .08 inches) are all acceptable.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2's Buckshot size table, what is the approximate diameter of "00 Buck" (American designation)?
questions.refText: 00 Buck — UK: SG, Inches: .33 ins, Metric: 8.4 mm, Typical Pellets Per Cartridge (12 ga. nominal): 9-12.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, using a compound such as glue or resin to bind birdshot or buckshot pellets together is:
o: Deemed to be in contravention of the IPSC rulebook definition of these ammunition types
Explicitly permitted to improve pattern performance
Permitted only in SG Open Division
questions.refText: 18. "Birdshot" and "Buckshot" are ammunition types where the shot contained therein easily separates. Any compound or substance, such as glue or resin, that binds the shot together is deemed to be in contravention of the IPSC rulebook definition of these ammunition types.

questions.q: According to Appendix E2, lead shot in shotgun ammunition is:
o: Permitted, subject to local environmental restrictions
Permitted only at Level I and II matches
Permitted only when used with frangible targets
questions.refText: 6. Lead shot — Permitted subject to local environmental restrictions.

questions.q: According to Appendix F1, which hand signal represents "Miss"?
questions.refText: Scoring Hand Signals — Alpha: Miss. Charlie: No-Shoot. Delta: Re-Score.

questions.refText: Scoring Hand Signals — Alpha: Miss. Charlie: No-Shoot. Delta: Re-Score.
